extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of drama/playwriting and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and judging tragic drama according to Aristotelian principles: unity of action, the minor unities (time/place), structure, and the qualities of the tragic hero that produce katharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action
rubrics_metrics.description: The only dramatic Unity enjoined by Aristotle: the whole series of events (thoughts, emotions, decisions, external events) must be causally connected and directed to a single end so that the action converges on a definite point — 'the end is linked to the beginning with inevitable certainty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity is revealed by causal connexion and a thread of purpose; parts must form an 'organic' structure (not a mechanical piecing together). All minor effects are subordinated to an ever growing unity; 'the supreme test of unity' is the powerful and concentrated impression produced when the whole meaning is discerned in the end. If Unity of Action is preserved, minor unities will generally follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic structure / σύστασις (synthesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition (σύστασις or σύνθεσις) of a play denotes a vital union of parts rather than mechanical piecing; scenes should lead (by logic) to what follows and contribute to the inevitable catastrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arbitrary or haphazard joining of incidents. Each scene should contribute its fraction of impulse toward the catastrophe; the structure should be 'necessary and harmonious' rather than merely mechanical. Quoted support: Lowell's idea that each scene should lead by logic to something that follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Time ('single revolution of the sun')
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle reports a prevailing practice that tragedy should 'as far as possible' confine the imaginary time of the dramatic action to a single revolution of the sun (interpreted variably as ~12 or 24 hours) — a generalisation of Greek stage practice rather than a strict rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is recorded as a prevailing usage with many historical exceptions; critics debated 12 vs 24 hours. Where strict equivalence is impossible, Aristotle allows 'probability' (εἰκός) as a corrective. Do not treat this as an absolute rule; compress time only insofar as it preserves the unity and verisimilitude necessary for the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Place
rubrics_metrics.description: A stage practice generally observed in Greek drama (but not enjoined in the Poetics): keeping the action in a continuous singular place supports the impression of unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity of Place is often deduced from Unity of Time and helped by the Chorus' constant presence. It may be relaxed (e.g., allow changes within a single town or avoid shifts within the same act), but arbitrary scene changes can disturb unity and the audience's illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration / Compression of Dramatic Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama should be a compact and serried whole: events are concentrated, intimately tied to character development, and presented as present representation rather than leisurely recital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin near the climax when appropriate (the beginning should often coincide with the beginning of the Complication). Avoid long episodes or digressions that dilute the dramatic thrust; the spectator's attention demands immediacy and a hastening toward the goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of multiplicity of plots (πολύμυθος) in drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama rejects multiplicity of incidents typical of epic (πολύμυθος); a play should not contain many independent minor actions but one controlling action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic may contain numerous episodes and retarding incidents, but the drama's tissue must be closer and more inevitable in sequence. Avoid double-threaded plots or multiple equal plots that undermine the unity of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety/poikilia appropriate to genre (epic vs drama)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic admits ποικιλία (embellishment and variety), many episodes, and retarding incidents; drama should avoid such variety when it disrupts unity and concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use episodic variety only in narrative/epic forms; in drama, retarding incidents that delay the dénouement risk weakening the dramatic compression and moral inevitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the Chorus in unity and time
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus forms an ideal bond between parts of the action, tending toward Unity of Place and Continuity of Time; choral odes can suspend outward action and idealise time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choral lyrics allow the poet to 'release us from the captivity of time'—the interval covered by a choral ode is flexible and may be valued as the poet chooses. Use the Chorus strategically to sustain unity or to mediate necessary temporal/scene shifts without breaking dramatic illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude / probability (εἰκός) where strict realism fails
rubrics_metrics.description: When strict observance of time/place equivalence is impossible, Aristotle supplies 'probability' as a device to maintain the audience's belief in the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse imitation with literal deception; probability should be used to preserve the sense of truthfulness in the action when compressing or altering real time/space. Critics warn against overreliance on 'cheating' the senses, but poetic imagination may legitimately suspend exact realism for artistic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin at the Complication / relation of Beginning to Complication
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'beginning' of the play should, ideally, also be the beginning of the Complication (the group of events preceding the decisive turn of fortune); sometimes τὰ ἔξωθεν (external incidents) may be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient practice often starts near the climax (as in Oedipus Tyrannus). While including external pre-supposed incidents is allowed, aim to present the action whose causal chain leads directly to the decisive turn and dénouement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic purpose: produce katharsis of pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of tragedy is to produce the katharsis (purging) of pity and fear; the plot must be capable of producing these emotions fully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot, character, and catastrophe must be arranged to evoke pity and fear rather than mere moral satisfaction. The tragic effect is distinct from the satisfaction of poetic justice (φιλάνθρωπον), which may belong more properly to comedy or other forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of the Tragic Hero — moral middle ground
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero should be 'a man who morally stands midway between the two extremes' — not eminently good nor wholly villainous; inclined to goodness but prone to error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid heroes who are eminently good (their suffering repels rather than evokes pity) or utterly bad (their misfortune satisfies moral indignation but lacks tragic quality). The hero's relative goodness makes his fall moving and morally intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of the Tragic Hero — flaw or fatal error (hamartia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Misfortune should result from some flaw of character or fatal error in conduct (not from deliberate vice), making the calamity intelligible and tragic rather than deserved retribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cause of the downfall should be neither pure vice nor wholly arbitrary misfortune; it should arise from human frailty or mistake so the audience feels pity and fear rather than simple moral vindication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of the Tragic Hero — high rank/fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero should be illustrious in rank and fortune, so that the signal nature of the catastrophe is more striking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High status intensifies the tragic reversal and the audience's response; choose protagonists whose fall has public and dramatic resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid happy endings and double catastrophes for tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A transition from adversity to prosperity (happy ending), or plots with a double thread yielding prosperity for the good and misfortune for the bad, generally fails to produce the proper tragic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although audiences may prefer poetic justice or happy resolutions, Aristotle argues true tragedy prefers the unhappy ending that yields katharsis; reward/punishment correspondence that merely satisfies the moral sense is more characteristic of comedy or other genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not subordinate inner logic to slavish observance of minor unities
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Action is the higher law; subordinating character development and inner consistency to rigid enforcement of time/place rules (as in some French practice) damages the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid compressing incidents or misplacing scenes merely to meet an external time/place rule if doing so sacrifices believable character motivation or the inner logic of events. Artistic coherence of character and causation should take priority.
